chunks: Types of sensors and uses. The question: Name some types of sensors. What are they used for?
Sensors come in many types, and the easiest way to sort them is by what they measure: temperature, motion, light, force and pressure, or electrical current.
Each type works by some physical effect that changes an electrical property, such as resistance or voltage.
Knowing the effect tells you how to read the sensor and where it can go wrong.
Think of a toolbox. A tape measure, a scale and a thermometer each answer a different question, and you pick the one that fits the job. Sensors are the same.
A thermistor and a thermocouple both measure temperature, but one changes its resistance and the other makes a tiny voltage, so they need different circuits.
The toolbox picture does not show that each tool also has a typical weakness.
Mechanism decides the readout.

Resistive sensors need excitation and a divider or bridge, capacitive and piezo sensors need charge amplifiers (very high impedance), photodiodes need transimpedance amps, thermocouples need tiny-signal amplification.
Sensor: a part that turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal. Thermistor: a resistor whose resistance changes strongly with temperature.
Thermocouple: two different metals joined together that make a tiny voltage when the joint is hot.
Strain gauge: a thin wire pattern whose resistance changes slightly when it is stretched.
Accelerometer and gyroscope: sensors for how fast speed changes and how fast something spins.
Say you want to read a room's temperature. Pick a 10 kilohms thermistor, a part that is 10 kilohms at 25 degrees Celsius, and put it in series with a fixed 10 kilohms resistor.
At 25 degrees Celsius the two are equal, so the point between them sits at half the supply voltage.
If the room warms, the thermistor's resistance falls (the usual kind does), and that middle voltage shifts, which a converter can read.
A thermocouple would instead give only a few millivolts and need an amplifier.
"I group sensors by measurand. Temperature: NTC thermistors, RTDs and thermocouples. Motion: accelerometers, gyros, encoders and Hall sensors.
Light: photodiodes and image sensors. Force and pressure: strain gauges in bridges and piezoresistive diaphragms. Electrical: shunts and Hall sensors for current.
Each has a principle, a typical readout and a typical weakness: thermistors are nonlinear and self-heat, thermocouples give microvolts, gyros drift, Hall sensors are disturbed by stray fields."
